decisions.rationale: RESEARCH establishes what each candidate documents and explicitly states that none of it establishes accuracy or resource behavior for this application; it also flags model licensing and long-recording behavior as open for the Swift package, and notes that whisper.cpp's documented platform breadth does not imply matching performance. Committing to one runtime before the bake-off would be a choice without evidence. Two adapters behind one port makes the choice a configuration outcome rather than a rewrite, and the second adapter is the Intel story anyway.

alternatives.option: whisper.cpp only
alternatives.tradeoff: One runtime, C API, broadest hardware coverage, no Swift package licensing question; C interop and manual memory management in the hot path, and Core ML execution paths need extra work.

alternatives.option: WhisperKit only
alternatives.tradeoff: Best toolchain fit and the least integration code; leaves Intel unsupported structurally and makes an unresolved licensing question load-bearing.

alternatives.option: Apple's built-in speech recognition
alternatives.tradeoff: No models to manage and no download; on-device availability and language coverage are controlled by the system, and model choice, which the requirements demand, is not exposed.

decisions.consequences: Two adapters to maintain and two sets of parameters to translate into the stable `params_json` schema. Results record which runtime produced them, so a runtime change is visible in History rather than confusing. Until the bake-off runs, no accuracy or latency claim is made anywhere.
decisions.reconsider_when: The bake-off shows one runtime dominating on accuracy, latency, memory, and licensing, at which point the loser becomes a maintenance decision rather than a hedge.

decisions.title: Generation runtime: llama.cpp embedded in a helper, GGUF models
decisions.choice: Embed llama.cpp as a library in `dictation-llm-helper`, loading GGUF models with Metal acceleration on Apple Silicon and CPU otherwise. Streaming tokens back over the socket pair for live rewrite feedback. No server binary.
decisions.rationale: RESEARCH records llama.cpp as providing local inference with Metal support and both library-oriented integration and server tooling, and asks that an embedded worker be compared against a local service including whether network access is possible. Embedding the library gives control over acquisition and lifecycle; GGUF gives access to the broad set of quantized models users already have, which matters because the requirements include user-supplied models.

alternatives.option: MLX-based generation
alternatives.tradeoff: Apple-native, actively developed, good Apple Silicon performance; a different model format, a smaller ecosystem of ready quantizations, and no Intel path.

alternatives.option: Core ML converted models
alternatives.tradeoff: System-managed execution and no vendored C++; conversion work per model, and user-supplied model support becomes impractical.

alternatives.option: The llama.cpp server on localhost
alternatives.tradeoff: Reuses upstream tooling; the reachability and forwarding concerns in D-003 apply directly.

decisions.consequences: Vendored C++ with the build time, pinning, and update discipline that implies. The helper must be built for the target architectures and signed as part of the app bundle. Quantization choice becomes a user-visible setting with a memory consequence, surfaced through the residency policy in D-027.
decisions.reconsider_when: MLX coverage of the quantized models users bring becomes comparable, or measured generation latency on the target machine is unacceptable and another runtime measurably beats it.

decisions.title: Model identity, staged installation, and compatibility checks
decisions.choice: Model identity is `(publisher name, revision string, SHA-256 over the ordered weight file set)`. Installation stages into `Models/.staging/<uuid>`, verifies size and hash, runs a load smoke test in the helper (load, then one second of silence through recognition or an eight-token generation), and only then atomically renames the directory into place and updates the manifest pointer. Compatibility is checked before activation against the installed runtime's descriptor: runtime kind, required runtime version range, quantization support, sample rate, declared context length. User-supplied models take the same path with user-entered manifest fields and the same smoke-test gate. Runtimes never load a model by name; they receive an absolute path to an activated directory.
decisions.rationale: Hashing the weights rather than trusting a name is what makes 'the same model' a checkable claim across a rename or a re-download. Staging plus atomic rename is what makes a failed download or import unable to replace a working installation: the live directory is never opened for writing during an install. The smoke test catches the common user-supplied failure (a quantization the installed runtime cannot read) at install time rather than mid-dictation. RESEARCH warns that a default runtime initialization may download models, so passing explicit paths is the enforcement point.

alternatives.option: Identity by file name or publisher identifier only
alternatives.tradeoff: No hashing cost on multi-gigabyte files; two different quantizations under one name become indistinguishable in History.

alternatives.option: Install in place and roll back on failure
alternatives.tradeoff: No staging space needed; a failure during the write leaves a corrupt live model, which is exactly the outcome the requirement forbids.

alternatives.option: Let the runtime's own downloader manage models
alternatives.tradeoff: Much less code; hands acquisition to a component that may download implicitly, which breaks the offline contract.

decisions.consequences: Installation needs free space for both the staged and the live copy, which the interface checks before starting. Hashing multi-gigabyte files takes time and is shown as a verification step. Failed user imports stay in staging with an attached error until dismissed, so staging needs its own cleanup in the launch sweep.
decisions.reconsider_when: Hashing time on large models becomes a usability problem, which would argue for incremental hashing during download rather than a separate pass.

decisions.title: Meetings: two captured streams, diarization as hypotheses, notes with citations
decisions.choice: Record microphone and system audio as separate files aligned by host time, so 'me' versus 'the call' is structural. Within a stream, diarization produces `speakerHypothesis {clusterId, confidence}` per segment; below the threshold the segment is labeled unattributed rather than assigned. Display names live in a separate cluster-to-name mapping, so renaming never rewrites model output, and re-running diarization keeps names where cluster ids are stable and asks where they are not. Notes are generated by a built-in mode over the timestamped transcript, chunked to the model's context budget, with each bullet citing a segment range and uncited bullets dropped in the reduce pass. Diarization is off unless a diarizer is installed and its evaluation row exists.
decisions.rationale: The requirement not to treat speaker identity as certain when the model gives insufficient evidence needs a representation that can express uncertainty, which is why confidence and an unattributed label are in the schema rather than a bare speaker name. Separating names from cluster ids means user edits and model output do not overwrite each other. RESEARCH names SpeakerKit as available in the Argmax package and notes its default initialization may download models, so its acquisition goes through the model store like everything else.

alternatives.option: Diarize a single mixed recording
alternatives.tradeoff: One file and one capture path; discards the certain channel-origin signal and makes the easiest attribution question (was that me?) an inference.

alternatives.option: Assign every segment to the nearest cluster regardless of confidence
alternatives.tradeoff: Clean-looking transcripts; confidently wrong attributions in meeting notes, which is the failure mode the requirements call out.

alternatives.option: Generate notes from the whole transcript in one pass
alternatives.tradeoff: Better global structure; exceeds context on long meetings and gives no way to check a bullet against the audio.

decisions.consequences: Two audio files per meeting and roughly double the storage. Notes quality depends on chunk boundaries, mitigated by overlapping windows. Dropping uncited bullets can remove a correct summary line that failed to cite; the reduce prompt therefore requires citations explicitly, and the drop rate is tracked in evaluation. Diarization error rate has not been measured and no attribution quality is claimed.
decisions.reconsider_when: Measured diarization error on mixed audio is close to the channel-separated result, or a diarizer exposes no usable confidence, in which case meetings ship with channel attribution only.

decisions.title: History: append-only results, full-text search, tombstones with job generation tokens
decisions.choice: One recording owns one audio artifact and many result rows, each recording its mode revision, model ids, and parameters. Reprocessing inserts a row and never mutates one; a user-movable pointer selects the displayed result. Search is FTS5 over result text with bm25 ranking and snippets. Deletion sets a tombstone and increments a generation counter; every worker carries `(recording_id, generation)` and its commit is a single transaction that aborts if the row is gone, tombstoned, or at a different generation. Hard deletion of rows and audio happens when the last job token is released, or at the next launch sweep.
decisions.rationale: 'A late worker response must not recreate a deleted recording' is only true if the existence check and the insert are the same transaction; any check-then-insert has a window. The generation counter additionally covers delete-then-recreate at the same identifier. Append-only results are what makes reprocessing under different models comparable rather than destructive, and what lets History explain how a result was produced.

alternatives.option: Hard delete immediately and let workers fail on missing rows
alternatives.tradeoff: No tombstone bookkeeping; a foreign key violation is a race outcome rather than a defined behavior, and scratch files are orphaned.

alternatives.option: Cancel workers and wait for acknowledgement before deleting
alternatives.tradeoff: No tombstone state to reason about; the user's delete blocks on a worker that may be mid-chunk, and a hung worker blocks it indefinitely.

alternatives.option: Overwrite the result on reprocessing
alternatives.tradeoff: One result per recording and a simpler list; comparing a new model against the old one becomes impossible, which is a stated use of reprocessing.

decisions.consequences: Deleted recordings occupy disk until their jobs release, so the interface reports 'deleting' rather than claiming space is reclaimed. FTS triggers must handle result deletion, covered by tests. Many results per recording needs a History detail view that makes the source transcript and the current result distinguishable at a glance.
decisions.reconsider_when: Result rows dominate database size, which would argue for storing older results compressed or on disk rather than inline.

decisions.title: Desktop behavior: menu bar surface, software input gain, media control with ownership tracking
decisions.choice: An NSStatusItem showing state, current mode, recent results, and settings, as the always-available surface. Microphone level is adjusted as software gain on captured buffers by default, with metering and a clipping indicator; setting the input device's hardware volume is opt-in. Media pausing checks whether the default output device is running before capture, posts a play/pause media key if so, and resumes afterwards only if the app sent the pause, the same output device is still default, the device is still idle, and under ten minutes have passed. Device volume is restored only if the current value equals the value the app set.
decisions.rationale: Software gain does not change a system setting the user might rely on elsewhere, so the default has no restore obligation at all. Where the app does change system state, 'restore only when we still own the change' is enforced by comparing against the value the app set rather than assuming it survived. The output-device running flag is a public CoreAudio property and avoids depending on a private media framework for the play-state check.

alternatives.option: Always set the input device hardware volume
alternatives.tradeoff: Improves the signal reaching every consumer including the recognizer; changes a setting other applications share, and a crash leaves it changed.

alternatives.option: Use the private MediaRemote framework for playback state and control
alternatives.tradeoff: Accurate per-application playback state and precise control; an undocumented interface that can break on any OS update and complicates notarization posture.

alternatives.option: Per-application scripting for known players
alternatives.tradeoff: Precise control of Music, Spotify, and similar; requires automation permission per application and covers only an enumerated list.

alternatives.option: Do not touch media playback
alternatives.tradeoff: Nothing to restore and nothing to get wrong; leaves background audio bleeding into recordings, which the requirement asks to address.

decisions.consequences: The running-somewhere flag cannot tell which application is playing or whether the media key reached it, so resume can be declined in ambiguous cases and the menu says playback was left alone. Software gain cannot rescue a signal already clipped at the hardware, which the clipping indicator makes visible so the user can lower device gain themselves.
decisions.reconsider_when: Users report that pausing frequently misses or that resume frequently declines, which would argue for per-application scripting for the players they actually use.

decisions.title: Shortcuts through one event tap, with per-mode bindings and a documented fallback
decisions.choice: A single `ShortcutRegistrar` owns a CGEventTap at the session level as a default (consuming) tap, handling keyDown, keyUp, and flagsChanged. Toggle starts and stops on keyDown. Push-to-talk arms on keyDown after a 200 ms hold (so a tap reads as a toggle) and finalizes on keyUp, with a watchdog that finalizes at the configured maximum hold if keyUp is lost to a disabled tap or a locked screen. Per-mode bindings register additional combinations that select the mode and start a session in one action. Conflicts within the app are detected at bind time; system conflicts are surfaced by a test-press step that reports if no event arrives. `kCGEventTapDisabledByTimeout` re-enables the tap. If the tap cannot be created, fall back to Carbon `RegisterEventHotKey` for toggle only and disable push-to-talk with an explanation.
decisions.rationale: Push-to-talk needs key-up and the ability to consume the hotkey so it does not reach the foreground application; only an active event tap provides both. The tap needs the Accessibility permission, which text delivery already requires, so it adds no new permission. The Carbon fallback keeps the application usable when the permission is missing, at the cost of the feature that needs key-up.

alternatives.option: Carbon RegisterEventHotKey only
alternatives.tradeoff: No Accessibility permission needed and reliable consumption; no key-up event, so push-to-talk cannot be implemented.

alternatives.option: NSEvent global monitors only
alternatives.tradeoff: Simple API with no tap lifecycle; events cannot be consumed, so the hotkey also reaches the foreground application.

alternatives.option: A separate tap per registered shortcut
alternatives.tradeoff: Isolated failure per shortcut; multiplies tap overhead on every keystroke and multiplies the timeout-disable handling.

decisions.consequences: The application sits on the keyboard event path, so its handler must stay fast; a slow handler gets the tap disabled by timeout, which the re-enable path treats as a monitored condition rather than an oddity. Secure input mode suppresses events entirely, which is why arming reports delivery-unavailable up front in that state.
decisions.reconsider_when: A supported API for global hotkeys with key-up appears, or event tap latency is measured to affect typing.

decisions.title: Model residency policy under a declared memory budget
decisions.choice: Budget the application at 8 GB peak on the 16 GB target. At most one speech model and one generation model resident, unloaded after ten idle minutes. Activation of a pairing whose declared footprints plus estimated KV cache exceed the budget is refused with the arithmetic shown and an explicit override. The provisional pass reuses the resident speech model rather than loading a second one when the sum would exceed the speech budget.
decisions.rationale: The specification forbids artificial quotas and requires honest reporting of limitations, which is different from ignoring the memory ceiling. Swapping on a 16 GB machine turns a latency problem into a system-wide stall, so the policy is stated up front with its arithmetic visible, and the user can override it because it is their machine.

alternatives.option: Load models on demand with no residency limit
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest and fastest when memory allows; on the stated target a large pairing plus a browser drives the machine into swap.

alternatives.option: Keep all selected models resident permanently
alternatives.tradeoff: Lowest per-session latency; several gigabytes held while the app is idle in the menu bar.

alternatives.option: Rely on the system's memory pressure notifications alone
alternatives.tradeoff: Adapts to actual conditions rather than declared sizes; reacts after the fact, when the stall has already happened.

decisions.consequences: First use after an idle period pays a model load, which the panel shows as a loading state. The budget is arithmetic over declared file sizes rather than measured resident size, so it is an assumption that the first measurement can invalidate in either direction. Memory pressure notifications are still observed and trigger early unload of idle models.
decisions.reconsider_when: Measured resident size differs materially from declared sizes, or the app is run on machines where the ceiling is not binding.

decisions.title: Egress control: no networking in inference paths, downloads isolated behind explicit user action
decisions.choice: Inference helpers contain no networking code and are checked for socket-API symbols in CI. Model downloads run only from an explicit user action, through a separate downloader component restricted to an allowlist of model hosts, writing only into the staging directory. Runtime initializers that can download are prohibited by a static check; runtimes always receive an absolute local path. Setup may offer downloads; routine operation performs none. Audio, transcripts, and context never cross a process boundary other than the local socket pair to a helper.
decisions.rationale: The specification requires that captured audio and transcripts stay on the Mac, that application context never reach external services, and that model loading not trigger implicit downloads. RESEARCH specifically notes that SpeakerKit's default initialization may download models. A guarantee enforced by code structure and a build-time check is verifiable; one enforced by careful calling conventions is not.

alternatives.option: Allow runtimes to fetch missing models automatically
alternatives.tradeoff: Better first-run experience with no model manager; makes network access a side effect of loading a model, which is the behavior the requirements forbid.

alternatives.option: Rely on App Sandbox network entitlement withholding
alternatives.tradeoff: System-enforced rather than structural; the application is unsandboxed for accessibility injection reasons, so the entitlement is not available as the enforcement mechanism.

alternatives.option: Ship no downloader at all and require manual model placement
alternatives.tradeoff: The strongest guarantee and the least code; makes first run considerably harder and pushes users toward downloading models through less careful means.

decisions.consequences: The downloader is a distinct component with its own permission story and its own tests. Users who want a model outside the allowlist import it as a local file, which goes through the same verification. The offline claim is testable: a full session under a network-denied profile is part of verification.
decisions.reconsider_when: The distribution and sandbox question in the open questions resolves differently, which changes which enforcement mechanism is available, not the requirement.

coverage.explanation: Global toggle and push-to-talk from another application come from one session-level event tap that can both observe key-up and consume the hotkey (D-026); push-to-talk uses a 200 ms hold to distinguish from a toggle tap and a watchdog to finalize if key-up is lost. Shortcuts are configurable, including per-mode bindings that select a mode and start a session in one action, with in-app conflict detection at bind time and a test-press step for system conflicts the app cannot enumerate. When the Accessibility permission is absent the tap cannot be created, so the app falls back to a Carbon hotkey for toggle and says that push-to-talk is unavailable rather than failing silently. Cancellation has a defined effect at every stage (D-007) because the stages are explicit states (D-006): arming discards, capturing discards audio by default, recognizing keeps audio and saves no partial transcript, refining drops the normalized result, rewriting keeps the normalized transcript and offers it, and delivering is cancellable only before the first event is posted. Cancellation reaches workers at chunk checkpoints through the scheduler (D-004), so it is prompt without leaving partial work committed.

The processed transcript is inserted through an injection ladder: accessibility set-value first, pasteboard plus Command-V next, synthesized Unicode keystrokes last for short text (D-009). Optional submission uses the modifier state sampled when the stop shortcut was released, and the Return is posted only when delivery went to the latched element through a path that posted events. The intended target is latched at arming and the focus-change policy is explicit (D-008): same element delivers, same application with a different element delivers by default, a different application holds and offers Deliver or Copy, and a departed application holds. The recording panel is non-activating so it cannot disturb the latch. Clipboard changes are handled by snapshotting items before writing and restoring after 300 ms only if the change count still matches, leaving newer user content alone and reporting a partial snapshot when items were too large to hold. Permissions denied or revoked route the result to History and the pasteboard with a named reason, and secure input suppresses synthesis entirely rather than dropping text into a password field. Duplicate delivery after a crash is prevented structurally (D-010): the attempt row is committed before any event is posted, and on launch pending or posted attempts become needs_review, never re-posted, because the paste path gives no confirmation that would make a retry safe.

A provisional live transcript is produced by a separate low-priority pass over a sliding window, and a waveform is drawn from a 10 ms RMS and peak envelope computed on the capture thread without allocation (D-011). The compact window is a non-activating, borderless panel at status-bar level that joins all spaces, is movable by its background, and is ordered front without becoming key so it cannot break the delivery latch. Placement is remembered as a fraction of the display's visible frame plus the display identifier, clamped to the primary display when the original display or frame is gone. Provisional text renders in a secondary style with a live label and is replaced by the final transcript in the primary style with a change highlight; the provisional result is discarded rather than promoted, because it was produced over partial context and is a different artifact (D-006). Recording and processing failures appear as a panel row with a short reason and one action, including the case where the scheduler declines the provisional pass while a batch job runs, which shows as preview paused rather than as a stalled transcript (D-004).

Four built-in modes cover ordinary dictation and task-specific output: Standard, Email, Note, and Meeting notes (D-013). Each declares its permitted transformations explicitly rather than describing them in prose: Standard is limited to punctuation, capitalization, optional disfluency removal, and vocabulary substitution, with no reordering or summarizing; Email adds template salutation and sign-off, paragraph structure, and register adjustment, with no new factual content; Note adds list and heading structure; Meeting notes permits summarization because that is its purpose, and is guarded by a citation requirement instead of a recall threshold. None of the four declares the ability to answer questions, and the output validator enforces that interrogatives present in the normalized transcript survive in order in the output, with a single stricter retry and then a fall back to the normalized transcript marked as a validator fallback (D-012). A mode that answered dictated questions would have to declare that capability, which would also make it visibly distinct in the mode indicator.

Users author prompts and formatting rules, and each custom mode selects its own local speech model and language model by identity, not by name (D-012, D-022). Every save produces a new content-addressed revision in an append-only chain, and every run pins the revision id into its RunManifest at arming along with the model ids, vocabulary revision, language setting, and translation flag (D-006). Work already in progress therefore reads its snapshot rather than live settings, so editing a mode or switching models while a recognition is running cannot change what the running job produces. Saved results keep pointing at the revision that produced them, and the History detail view names that revision and can diff it against the current one, so a later edit cannot silently change the meaning of an earlier result. Custom modes declare their permitted transformations like built-ins do, so the same validator applies; duplicating a built-in to customize it carries the built-in's declared transformation set as a starting point.

Rules match on the foreground application's bundle identifier and, where readable, the website URL, and are evaluated once at arming with first match winning over a user-ordered list (D-014). Conflicts resolve by that user order, with specificity (host plus path, then host, then bundle identifier, then any) as the tiebreak within equal priority, and the settings editor flags rules that can never fire because an earlier rule shadows them. When context cannot be obtained, because automation permission for a browser is denied, the browser does not expose its URL, or screen recording is off, rules requiring that input do not match and evaluation continues; if nothing matches, the user's default mode applies. The selected mode is latched for the session, so it cannot change mid-sentence. The effective mode is shown in the recording panel and the menu bar for every session, along with whether it came from a matching rule or from the fallback, which is what keeps the current mode apparent (D-011).

User terminology and names enter at four defined points with a fixed order relative to recognition and language processing (D-015). Before recognition, selected terms are placed in the decoder's prompt slot, bounded by the runtime's limit and chosen by mode relevance and recency; this shifts decoding probabilities and is described in the interface as exactly that, with no claim that adding a name guarantees recognition under all conditions, because the mechanism is a prompt rather than a decoding constraint (D-020). After recognition, configurable text replacements run deterministically over the source transcript with longest-match-first, word-boundary-aware, case-preserving, non-overlapping, single-pass semantics. Filler removal is a separate pass after replacement, toggleable per mode. After generation, the replacement table is applied once more and the validator checks that vocabulary terms survived, because a language model will sometimes normalize an unusual proper noun back to a common word and the user's spelling should win. The source transcript and the normalized transcript are both retained, so the effect of each stage is inspectable.

Three optional sources are sampled at arming in parallel against a 200 ms deadline: focused-element text and selection plus window title through accessibility, one frame of the focused window through ScreenCaptureKit with Vision text recognition when opted in, and the first text item on the pasteboard (D-016). Sampling once at arming makes a run reproducible and bounds the cost; anything that misses the deadline is omitted and recorded as omitted. Retention defaults to a digest, byte length, and source kind rather than the text, so the library does not accumulate copies of unrelated documents and screens, while a later reprocess can still report that the original context is unavailable; retaining the text is opt-in per mode, visible in History, and deleted with the recording. Missing permissions produce named degraded states: no screen recording means no screen context and no system audio while everything else continues; no accessibility means no focused-element text. Context is supplied as data, fenced in a per-run random delimiter and labeled as reference material with mode instructions before it and the task restated after, and the output validator is the enforcement that it did not become instructions, since framing alone is not a guarantee. Context never leaves the machine, because it is only ever passed over the local socket pair to a helper with no networking code (D-028).

Recognition language is set per mode to an explicit code or to automatic detection using the runtime's language identification with its probability; below the confidence threshold the run is recorded as undetermined, the mode's default language is used, and the panel shows that this happened (D-017). Translation into English is a separate declared operation that produces a new result row referencing the source transcript, which is never overwritten, so a retained translation or rewrite always sits beside the words that were actually spoken. Recognition and rewriting are evaluated by different methods, word error rate for the first and a human rubric for the second, and reported separately, because a rewrite score cannot distinguish a mis-recognized word from a badly reworded sentence. Language compatibility is declared per model in its manifest and checked at activation against the installed runtime (D-022, D-020); the interface attributes those claims to the model publisher and marks them unmeasured until an evaluation row exists, so no language coverage is promised on the strength of documentation alone.

Microphone (AVAudioEngine), system audio (ScreenCaptureKit), and imported audio and video files (AVAssetReader) all implement one `AudioSource` port emitting 16 kHz mono Float32 buffers plus a descriptor stating whether the source is live or seekable (D-018). The initial format matrix is what the system decoders cover: wav, aiff, caf, mp3, m4a in AAC and ALAC, mp4, m4v, and mov. The extension mechanism is a `DecoderProvider` port with an out-of-process command-line decoder adapter the user enables and points at an installed binary, run with no network access and piping raw PCM, so unusual formats are reachable without bundling a general decoder. Files decode in 30-second windows, so peak audio residency is one window plus the ring regardless of file length, and a three-hour import does not need memory proportional to its decoded duration; the memory ceiling is an assertion in the test suite and the measurement has not been taken. A failed import leaves its source unchanged because the import path opens the source read-only, copies into the session directory, and commits the History row only after the artifact is complete; on failure the session directory is removed and no row exists (D-019). Imports run in the batch lane and yield to interactive dictation at chunk boundaries (D-004).

A meeting captures microphone and system audio as two files aligned by host time, so the distinction between the local speaker and the remote participants is structural rather than inferred (D-023). Within a stream, diarization assigns each segment a cluster hypothesis with a confidence, and segments below the threshold are labeled unattributed rather than assigned to the nearest cluster, which is how the design avoids treating speaker identity as certain when the model provides insufficient evidence. Editing speaker names writes to a separate cluster-to-name mapping, so a rename never alters model output and re-running diarization preserves names where cluster ids are stable and asks where they are not. Timestamped notes are generated locally by a built-in mode over the diarized transcript, chunked to the language model's context budget with overlapping windows, where each bullet cites a segment range and uncited bullets are dropped in the reduce pass. The runtime choices are explicit: which diarizer is installed, which language model generates notes, and both are subject to the residency budget that keeps a long meeting from driving the machine into swap (D-027). Evaluation methods are named (diarization error rate on a labeled internal set, a human rubric plus automatic citation validity for notes) and have not been run, so no attribution quality is claimed. Meetings, their two audio artifacts, and their notes are ordinary History entries under the same retention and deletion rules (D-024).

Recordings are searchable through an FTS5 index over result text with bm25 ranking and snippets, and playable from the stored audio artifact (D-005, D-024). Reprocessing through a different model or mode inserts a new result row referencing the same recording, carrying the mode revision, speech and language model ids, and parameters that produced it (D-006); prior results are never mutated, and a user-movable pointer decides which result the list shows. The relationship between original audio and successive results is therefore one-to-many with full provenance on each result. Retention defaults to keeping everything, with optional age-based, size-based, and drop-audio-keep-text policies that show what they will remove before the first run. Deletion while processing is active sets a tombstone, increments a generation counter, and signals cancellation; every worker carries the recording id and generation from admission, and its commit is a single transaction that aborts if the row is missing, tombstoned, or at a different generation. A late worker response therefore cannot recreate a deleted recording, because the existence check and the insert cannot be separated. Audio files and rows are reclaimed once the last job token is released or at the next launch sweep, and the interface reports the interim state as deleting rather than claiming the space is already free.

A model library browses and manages installed speech and language models with their declared capabilities, sizes, and the runtime each belongs to (D-022). Identity is the publisher name, revision string, and a SHA-256 over the ordered weight file set, so two quantizations under the same name are distinguishable and a result in History can name exactly what produced it. Compatibility is checked before activation against the installed runtime's descriptor: runtime kind, required version range, quantization support, sample rate, declared context length. User-supplied models take the same path with user-entered manifest fields and the same load smoke test as the gate, so an unreadable quantization fails at install rather than mid-dictation. Installation stages into a separate directory, verifies, smoke-tests in the helper, and only then atomically renames into place, so a failed download or import cannot replace a working installation; a failed user import stays in staging with its error attached. Model loading never triggers a download, because runtimes receive absolute paths to activated directories and initializers that can fetch are prohibited by a build-time check, with acquisition confined to an explicitly invoked downloader on an allowlist (D-028). Replacing a runtime has bounded effect because runtimes are separate adapter targets and helper binaries (D-002, D-003, D-020, D-021), each owning its own models subtree so storage cost is attributable and removable, and each publishing a parameter schema the settings interface renders generically so a new runtime adds no bespoke screens. Activation of a model pairing whose declared footprints exceed the memory budget is refused with the arithmetic shown and an explicit override (D-027).

A menu bar status item is the always-available surface, showing current state, the effective mode, recent results, and settings, and it complements the recording panel rather than duplicating it (D-011, D-025). Microphone level adjustment is software gain applied to captured buffers by default, with metering and a clipping indicator, so the common case changes no system state and has nothing to restore; setting the input device's hardware volume is opt-in. Optional pausing of media playback checks whether the default output device is running before capture, using a public CoreAudio property rather than a private framework, and posts a play/pause media key when something is playing. Restoration happens only while the app still owns the change: playback resumes only if the app sent the pause, the same output device is still default, the device is still idle, and under ten minutes have elapsed; device volume is restored only if the current value still equals the value the app set. Competing applications and manual user edits therefore result in the app declining to restore and saying so in the menu, rather than overwriting a state someone else established. The macOS baseline and the public APIs these behaviors rely on are fixed by D-001, with anything newer gated behind availability checks and a defined fallback.

open_questions.question: Which speech runtime is selected, and does the license of the weights we would offer for download permit that distribution? RESEARCH establishes what WhisperKit and whisper.cpp document but explicitly states that documentation does not establish accuracy or resource behavior, and it flags model licensing and long-recording behavior as unexamined.
open_questions.resolution: Run the bake-off before phase 2 completes: both adapters against the same audio corpus (30-second dictation, 10-minute session, 3-hour meeting) on the target Apple Silicon machine, recording word error rate by language, time to final transcript, peak resident size, and behavior at chunk boundaries, with runtime revision, model revision, quantization, and machine specification attached to every row. In parallel, review the license of each candidate model distribution for redistribution and for offering as a download. Until both are answered, build against the `SpeechRecognizer` port with the whisper.cpp adapter as the reference implementation, and make no accuracy or latency claim in the product.

open_questions.question: Does the application ship unsandboxed under Developer ID (which the accessibility injection and session event tap appear to require), and if so what mechanism reliably denies network access to the inference helpers, given that per-process seatbelt initialization is deprecated?
open_questions.resolution: Spike before phase 0 ends, because it determines the entitlements files, the helper launch path, and how the offline contract is enforced. Build a helper, launch it under a restrictive profile, and assert that an outbound connect fails; separately assert that a helper built without networking code contains no socket-API symbols. If the profile mechanism proves unusable, the enforcement becomes the symbol scan plus the network-denied integration test, and the limitation is stated in the product rather than implied to be system-enforced. If sandboxing turns out to be viable with the required accessibility behavior, prefer it and record the change against D-003 and D-028.

open_questions.question: Which local diarizer is used for meetings, under what license, and does it expose a confidence signal the design can threshold on? RESEARCH names SpeakerKit within the Argmax package and notes that its default initialization may download models.
open_questions.resolution: Resolve before phase 8 begins, since the meetings data model depends on the answer. Evaluate the candidate's license and its per-segment outputs against a labeled internal meeting set, reporting diarization error rate and the proportion of segments falling below threshold. Confirm that a model-folder configuration prevents any download. If no usable confidence signal exists, meetings ship with channel attribution only and diarization stays off until a candidate that exposes one is available; the schema already represents that state.

open_questions.question: Can the provisional live transcription pass run alongside capture without dropping audio or degrading the final pass on the target machine?
open_questions.resolution: Measure during phase 2 alongside the bake-off: run capture with and without the provisional pass and compare dropped buffer counts, final word error rate, and time to final transcript. If the cost is material, the live preview degrades to waveform plus a voice-activity indicator, which the panel already has a state for.

open_questions.question: Which browsers expose the current URL through accessibility, and which require automation permission or provide nothing?
open_questions.resolution: Enumerate per browser during phase 6 and record a dated table. The rule engine already treats an unreadable URL as a non-match rather than an error, so an incomplete table degrades to bundle-identifier rules and the default mode instead of blocking the feature.

open_questions.question: Is FTS5 compiled into the system SQLite on the macOS 14 baseline?
open_questions.resolution: A one-line runtime check during phase 0 setup. If absent, build GRDB against a bundled SQLite, accepting a larger binary and an update obligation; record the change against D-005.

open_questions.question: How does the chosen speech runtime behave on a three-hour input: does chunked feeding introduce boundary errors, and does resident size stay flat across the run? RESEARCH raises long-recording suitability as needing examination.
open_questions.resolution: Covered by the phase 7 import test, which samples resident size across a three-hour file and compares transcripts at chunk boundaries against overlapping-window output. Chunked feeding is already the design, so the exposure is boundary quality rather than memory, and overlap size is the tuning knob.

open_questions.question: Is an 8B-class instruct model at 4-bit quantization good enough for the Email and Meeting notes modes on the 16 GB target, or does a smaller model with tighter prompts do better once the output validator is applied?
open_questions.resolution: Score two or three model sizes against the fidelity corpus during phase 4 using the human rubric, and record validator fallback rates per model. The result sets the recommended default pairing; the model selection is per mode either way, so a wrong initial default is a settings change rather than a design change.
